site.name: vlip
site.desc: A small Lisp dialect implemented in V, built around an explicit CEK machine with real tail calls and an embeddable core.
ui.untranslated: This section is not yet translated into your language; it is shown in English. Translations are welcome.
ui.footer: vlip is a Lisp dialect implemented in V. Early, and honest about what does not work yet.
home.title: A Lisp for V, with tail calls that are actually free
home.sub: A small Lisp dialect built on an explicit CEK machine. Tail calls reuse their frame instead of pushing one, so a loop is a loop and not a stack that grows until it dies.
home.p1.b: A quarter of a million iterations end with an empty continuation stack. Mutual recursion tail-calls too, which is the part most trampolines skip.
home.p2.b: Evaluation is a data structure you can inspect, not a recursive function you have to trust. Every step is counted, and every limit is a field you can set.
home.p3.b: The machine is a library with no global state. print output is collected into a field, so a host can capture it rather than fight it.
home.status1: Working: the reader, closures, arithmetic, branching, loop, dotimes, letrec, cond, case, and proper tail calls including mutual recursion.
home.status2: Working: let, let*, letrec, rest parameters, and keywords that are callable, so (:a {:a 1}) is a lookup. Not yet: match, structs, modules and macros. Each one is named in the repository rather than quietly missing.
features.title: Features
features.sub: What the machine does today, and what it is built to do next.
features.tco.b: A call in tail position reuses the current continuation frame instead of pushing one. Self-recursion and mutual recursion both loop in constant space.
features.machine.b: Control, environment, and value are separate machine fields. Recursion in the evaluator is a tail call, so the V stack cannot overflow on a vlip loop.
features.truthy.b: As in R5RS and Clojure: 0, the empty string, nil, and () are all true. Ruby and JavaScript say the opposite, which is why newcomers relearn this.
features.forms.b: A small core that everything else desugars into, so each derived form gets tail calls for free instead of needing its own trampoline.
features.errors.b: Step and continuation-depth limits are fields on the machine, not constants, so a host can bound untrusted code.
features.embed.b: One Machine value holds everything. Two can run side by side with no interference, which is what makes embedding and testing possible.
features.depth1: A tree-walking evaluator written as a recursive function runs out of C stack before it runs out of vlip stack. Every non-tail vlip call becomes another V frame, so the host's limit becomes your limit.
features.depth2: Writing the evaluator as an explicit machine with its own heap stack moves that boundary somewhere you can see. The cost is a step counter and a dispatch loop. The benefit is that the numbers in the table below are measured rather than hoped for.
features.benchNote: A stack depth of zero at the end is the whole claim. Without real tail calls that column would hold the iteration count instead. Every number here is produced by the test suite that CI runs, so none of them can drift away from the implementation unnoticed.
docs.title: Documentation
docs.sub: A reference for what the interpreter accepts today. Where something is not implemented yet, the reference says so rather than omitting it.
docs.val.nil.d: The absence of a value, and the result of a branch with no alternative.
docs.val.bool.d: True or false. Only false is falsey.
docs.val.string.d: An immutable sequence of bytes, written as text.
docs.val.sym.d: An interned name. Evaluating one looks it up.
docs.val.kw.d: An interned name that evaluates to itself.
docs.val.list.d: A cons cell: a value and the rest of the list.
docs.val.table.d: An immutable string-keyed map with sorted keys, so output is stable.
docs.val.closure.d: A procedure and the environment it captured.
docs.val.prim.d: A built-in procedure implemented in V.
docs.core.if.d: Evaluate the test, then one branch. With no alternative the result is nil.
docs.core.define.d: Bind a name in the current frame. A list target defines a procedure.
docs.core.set.d: Assign to the frame that owns the binding, so a closure sees the change on its next call.
docs.core.lambda.d: Create a procedure. fn is a synonym.
docs.core.begin.d: Evaluate in order, return the last. The last form keeps its tail position, so tail calls inside a begin are still tail calls.
docs.core.let.d: Bind names and evaluate the body in a new frame. let binds simultaneously, let* in order, letrec with every name visible to every value.
docs.core.and.d: Short-circuit. Return the first falsey value, or the last value.
docs.core.quote.d: Return the form itself instead of evaluating it. The apostrophe is shorthand.
docs.der.when.d: Run the body only if the test is true, otherwise nil.
docs.der.unless.d: Run the body only if the test is false, otherwise nil.
docs.der.cond.d: Try clauses in order and take the first whose test is true. => separates test from body.
docs.der.case.d: Compare one value against a list of candidates per clause.
docs.der.loop.d: A named let: bind the variable, run the body while the test holds, and advance the variable each round.
docs.der.dotimes.d: loop with an implicit counter from zero.
docs.truthy1: Only #f is false. The number zero, the empty string, nil, and the empty list are all true. This matches R5RS and Clojure, and deliberately does not match Ruby, JavaScript, or Python.
docs.truthy2: The rule matters more than it looks. A language that treats 0 as falsey makes every numeric result a potential branch, which is why code in those languages needs explicit nil checks that vlip code does not.
docs.p.arith.d: Whole numbers, with promotion when a float is involved.
docs.p.logic.d: Negation. and and or are forms, not primitives, because they short-circuit.
docs.p.list.d: Build and take apart cons cells.
docs.p.seq.d: Take a procedure and a list, and return a new list.
docs.p.io.d: Write to the machine's output buffer, not straight to a terminal, so a host can capture it.
docs.wip1: match, match*, structs, modules and macros are written in the examples and do not yet evaluate. Each one is named in the repository rather than quietly missing.
docs.wip2: The bracket question is settled: [ ] is read by position, not by a reader flag. In the second slot of let, let* and letrec it is a binding group, and everywhere else it is a vector literal. Both [a 1] and (a 1) are accepted.
guides.title: Guides
guides.sub: From a clone to something that runs, in five steps.
guides.s1.b: Clone, then compile the CLI. Use -cc gcc: the default C backend fails on this checkout, and CI uses the same flag so the two cannot disagree.
guides.s2.b: A lambda takes a parameter list and a body. Define binds it. map applies it to each element.
guides.s3.b: cond takes clauses in order and runs the body of the first whose test is true. The else clause catches the rest.
guides.s4.t: Write a loop that is not a loop
guides.s4.b: An ordinary recursive function whose call is in tail position. The continuation stack does not grow, so depth is limited by memory rather than by the stack.
guides.s5.b: loop is a named let: it advances the variable for you. Same constant space, less to get wrong.
guides.next1: The examples directory is the best next stop. Six programs, and they are the specification the interpreter is written against: if the interpreter and an example disagree, one of them is wrong and the example usually wins.
guides.next2: After that, the roadmap. It names what is broken, what is next, and which order those things have to happen in.
guides.help1: Bug reports and pull requests are welcome, including translations. The contributing guide covers how to build, how to run the tests, and the branch layout.
